nature-econ-378.q: What did a free market mean to classical economists such as Adam Smith?
nature-econ-378.a: A market free of privilege, monopolies and artificial scarcities.

nature-econ-358.q: What does a price elasticity of demand of -2 mean?
nature-econ-358.a: A one percent price rise cuts the quantity demanded by two percent.

nature-econ-395.q: What tools can governments use to intervene in prices and deal with externalities?
nature-econ-395.a: Price ceilings or floors, such as minimum wages, or Pigovian taxes.

nature-econ-407.q: In what three ways do prices match buyers and sellers?
nature-econ-407.a: As an incentive, as a signal and as a way of rationing resources.

nature-econ-349.q: Why can a monopoly charge a price well above its marginal cost?
nature-econ-349.a: Because it lacks competition and close substitutes, so it can earn high profits.

nature-econ-392.q: Why do barriers to entry matter most in antitrust policy?
nature-econ-392.a: By protecting incumbents and restricting competition, they can distort prices.

nature-econ-343.q: If a tax falls legally on sellers, who largely ends up paying it?
nature-econ-343.a: Buyers, through higher prices; who legally pays the tax does not matter.

nature-econ-404.q: Why are supply elasticities usually positive?
nature-econ-404.a: Because a higher price encourages more production.

nature-econ-355.q: What did Hayek argue is the point of laissez-faire?
nature-econ-355.a: To keep the unique information that a price carries.

nature-econ-375.q: What does a monopsonist do about the price it pays for an input?
nature-econ-375.a: It sets the price instead of taking it from the market, choosing a point on the input's supply curve.

nature-econ-372.a: A good used to make another, final good.

nature-econ-400.q: What happens when a price ceiling is set below the market equilibrium price?
nature-econ-400.a: It leads to a shortage of supply.

nature-econ-309.q: In macroeconomics, when is the long run?
nature-econ-309.a: When prices, contracted wages and expectations have fully adjusted.

nature-econ-301.q: How do cartels create artificial shortages?
nature-econ-301.a: Through low production quotas, stockpiling and marketing quotas.

nature-econ-302.q: In the Cournot model, how do prices and quantities under duopoly compare with monopoly?
nature-econ-302.a: Prices are lower and quantities higher under duopoly than under monopoly.

nature-econ-623.q: What is the hold-up problem in the property rights approach to the firm?
nature-econ-623.a: Since deals will be renegotiated, each party expects only part of the return on its investment and so invests too little.

nature-econ-321.q: What curve does the adoption of a new technology usually follow?
nature-econ-321.a: An S-shaped curve: slow at first, then rapid, then levelling off as the market saturates.

nature-econ-168.q: After whom is Pareto efficiency named, and what was he?
nature-econ-168.a: Vilfredo Pareto, an Italian engineer and economist who used it to study economic efficiency and income distribution.

nature-econ-173.q: What does distributive justice look at, in contrast with fair process?

nature-econ-191.q: Why need a Pareto efficient market outcome not be fair?
nature-econ-191.a: Because many Pareto efficient allocations exist, including one where one person owns everything.

nature-econ-179.q: What field did Arrow found with his impossibility theorem of 1950?
nature-econ-179.a: Modern social choice theory, which studies how to combine preferences across a society.

nature-econ-161.q: What does the max-min social welfare function show about society's attitude?
nature-econ-161.a: An extreme aversion to uncertainty, caring only about the worst position anyone could face.

nature-econ-187.q: What does the second welfare theorem rely on to reach a desired efficient outcome?

nature-econ-177.q: What is the chicken-and-egg problem with alternative fuels?
nature-econ-177.a: Stations won't sell a fuel until such cars exist, and people won't buy the cars until stations exist.

nature-econ-852.q: What does the liberty principle, the first principle, give everyone?
nature-econ-852.a: Equal access to basic rights and liberties.

nature-econ-189.q: Why may an alcohol tax be a Pareto improvement when moral hazard is present?
nature-econ-189.a: Because it can reduce car accidents.

nature-econ-186.q: What can happen in overlapping-generations models when people save?
nature-econ-186.a: People may save more than is socially optimal, causing dynamic inefficiency.

nature-econ-198.q: What is a common view about the costs of tax-funded projects in a cost-benefit analysis?
nature-econ-198.a: They should be scaled up by the marginal cost of funds.

nature-econ-210.q: What did Coase argue would happen if there were no costs of making deals?
nature-econ-210.a: People would bargain their way to the most efficient use of resources whatever the starting legal rights.

nature-econ-289.q: Under strict liability, when is someone who keeps something inherently dangerous liable for damage?
nature-econ-289.a: Regardless of how carefully it was guarded.

nature-econ-640.q: What are environmental goods a sub-category of?

nature-econ-651.q: What did Aristotle observe about what is common to many?
nature-econ-651.a: That it is taken least care of.
